guise

rhymes with 'wise' — a guise is the 'wise,' or manner, in which someone presents themselves, often falsely. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Guise is an outward appearance or costume, especially one meant to conceal someone's true identity.

Under the guise of a simple repairman, the detective slipped into the mansion unnoticed.

Worked Example

A con artist knocks on doors dressed in a utility company uniform, carrying a clipboard and a badge, and tells homeowners he needs to check their water meter, when really he's casing the house for a robbery.

That false outward identity, put on specifically to hide someone's real purpose, is exactly what a guise is. Unlike 'uniform,' which can be worn honestly, a guise is specifically meant to mislead.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disguise: A disguise is a physical costume or altered look -- the wig, the borrowed uniform, the fake badge -- put on to hide who you are. A guise can be subtler than a disguise: any outward appearance or role someone adopts to conceal a true identity or purpose.

pretext: A pretext is a false reason given to hide the real one -- claiming a headache to leave a dull party early. A guise is a false appearance worn rather than a reason given: you operate under a guise, but you offer a pretext.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

true identity: a person's real, unhidden self

honesty: the quality of being truthful and open

Where it sits · how actively the false front is performed — facade → guise → pretense

facade vs. guise: Facade is broader than guise -- a facade can be any false front, even a building's, while guise specifically refers to a false appearance a person adopts.

pretense vs. guise: Pretense can feel more deliberate than guise: guise focuses on the false appearance itself, while pretense emphasizes the ongoing act of pretending.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — guis-/wis-

root — guis-/wis-: manner, way, fashion (Old French/Germanic)

Put it together

Put it together: Guise comes from Old French guise, 'manner, way, fashion,' from a Germanic root also seen in the English suffix '-wise' (as in likewise, otherwise). A guise is, at its root, simply the 'way' or 'manner' someone appears -- which is exactly why it can be used to mean a false appearance.

Use the root in a new word: otherwise

Use the root in a new word: otherwise: He said he was busy; otherwise, he would have joined us for dinner.
